pharm: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication and causing bactericidal cell death across a broad Gram-positive and Gram-negative spectrum.
quick: Pazufloxacin mesylate 500 mg-1000 mg IV infusion twice daily (per Japanese/Indian labels)
IV product not affected by meals; give as slow infusion
Avoid - fluoroquinolone class effects on cartilage
Avoid; fluoroquinolones may pass into milk
Reduce dose / lengthen interval in renal impairment
Renal function, tendons, QT/arrhythmia, glucose, CNS effects
summary: Pazufloxacin (pazufloxazin) is a fluoroquinolone antibacterial used mainly as an intravenous (mesylate) preparation in Japan and some Asian markets, and orally in some regions, for serious bacterial infections such as respiratory, urinary, and intra-abdominal infections and sepsis. It is bactericidal, inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. It is not an FDA-approved drug in the United States. As a fluoroquinolone it shares class risks including tendinitis/tendon rupture, QT prolongation, CNS effects, peripheral neuropathy, dysglycemia, and aortic events; it requires renal dose adjustment.
indications: Treatment of susceptible bacterial infections including respiratory tract infections (pneumonia)
Complicated urinary tract infections and pyelonephritis
Sepsis and other serious systemic bacterial infections (per regional labeling)

dosage.d: 500 mg infused over ~30-60 minutes twice daily; may increase to 1000 mg twice daily for severe/resistant infections
Reduce dose and/or lengthen dosing interval according to creatinine clearance
Per regional product label (e.g., region-specific oral dosing)

admin: Administer the IV (mesylate) solution as a slow intravenous infusion over about 30-60 minutes
Adjust dose in renal impairment based on creatinine clearance
Ensure adequate hydration to reduce crystalluria risk
Separate from di-/trivalent cation products (antacids, iron, calcium, sucralfate) for any oral form to avoid chelation
Counsel patients to stop and report tendon pain, swelling, or new neurologic/psychiatric symptoms
moa: Pazufloxacin is a fluoroquinolone that inhibits two essential bacterial type II topoisomerases: DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II), the primary target in Gram-negative bacteria, and topoisomerase IV, often the primary target in Gram-positive bacteria. By trapping these enzymes on DNA, it prevents the supercoiling, replication, transcription, and repair of bacterial DNA, leading to double-strand breaks and rapid bactericidal killing. It is active against a broad range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative aerobes.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to pazufloxacin or other fluoroquinolones
History of tendon disorders related to fluoroquinolone use
Concurrent QT-prolonging conditions where fluoroquinolones are contraindicated (per label)
relative: Known QT prolongation, uncorrected hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, or concomitant QT-prolonging drugs
History of seizures or CNS disorders

preg: Fluoroquinolones are generally avoided in pregnancy because of concerns about effects on developing cartilage and limited safety data. Use pazufloxacin in pregnancy only if there is no safer alternative and the benefit outweighs the risk.
lact: Fluoroquinolones may be excreted into breast milk and pose theoretical risks to the infant's developing joints. Avoid use during breastfeeding or discontinue nursing during therapy.
renal: Pazufloxacin is eliminated largely by the kidneys; clearance falls in renal impairment. Reduce the dose and/or extend the dosing interval according to creatinine clearance to avoid accumulation and toxicity.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment. As with other fluoroquinolones, monitor for rare hepatotoxicity and discontinue if signs of liver injury develop.

major: QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics) - additive QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk
Theophylline / NSAIDs - increased CNS stimulation and seizure risk (fluoroquinolone class effect)
moderate: Antidiabetic agents (insulin, sulfonylureas) - risk of hypo- or hyperglycemia
Corticosteroids - increased risk of tendon rupture, especially in elderly
minor: Di-/trivalent cations (antacids, iron, calcium, magnesium, sucralfate, zinc) - chelation reduces absorption of any oral form; separate dosing
interactions.food: IV product unaffected by food; for oral forms, separate from mineral supplements/antacids and dairy.
interactions.diagnostics: May affect blood glucose and prolong QT interval; can alter coagulation parameters with warfarin.

serious: Central nervous system effects (seizures, psychosis, confusion)

monitoring: ECG/QT in at-risk patients and electrolytes (K, Mg)
CNS and peripheral neuropathy symptoms; signs of C. difficile colitis
counsel: This is a strong antibiotic; complete the full course even if you feel better
Stop and seek care immediately if you develop tendon, joint, or muscle pain or swelling, or new numbness/tingling
Report fainting, palpitations, severe diarrhea, mood or sleep changes, or signs of low/high blood sugar
Avoid taking antacids, iron, calcium, or dairy close to any oral dose, and protect skin from strong sunlight
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have epilepsy, heart rhythm problems, or an aneurysm
pk: Bactericidal activity begins shortly after infusion
Store IV product per label, protected from light; do not freeze
pearls: Not FDA-approved in the United States; marketed mainly in Japan/India (IV mesylate) - dosing reflects those labels, not an FDA label
Shares all fluoroquinolone class warnings: tendon rupture, QT prolongation, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, dysglycemia, and aortic risk
Predominantly renally cleared - always adjust dose for renal impairment
Avoid in children, pregnancy, and breastfeeding because of cartilage toxicity concerns
Separate any oral form from antacids/iron/calcium to prevent chelation and treatment failure
missed: For the IV product, doses are given by a healthcare professional; if a scheduled dose is delayed, it is given as soon as feasible while maintaining the interval. For any oral form, take a missed dose when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, then skip it - do not double up.
overdose: Overdose may cause exaggerated adverse effects including CNS excitation/seizures, QT prolongation, and GI symptoms. There is no specific antidote; manage with supportive care, ECG and electrolyte monitoring, seizure precautions, and adequate hydration. Hemodialysis removes little drug. Contact a poison control center.
